hook-0-1mbojfw.text: Everything in the universe is flying apart.

hook-1-1sx38ng.text: And here's the weird part. It's speeding up.

hook-2-sliaon.text: Physicists call whatever is doing this: dark energy.

hook-3-9x4o7z.text: It makes up about seventy percent of everything. And nobody knows what it is.

hook-5-1ushcjw.text: What if nothing is pushing the universe apart?

hook-6-e8aqrd.text: What if something is pulling it?

problem-0-1xzrj9o.text: In 1998, two teams measured distant exploding stars, called type 1A supernovas.

problem-1-rrnufw.text: They looked too dim. They were farther away than a slowing universe would allow.

problem-2-9kz4xc.text: The fix was a cosmological constant, Lambda: energy built into empty space itself.

problem-3-18dbekq.text: Add invisible dark matter, and you get today's standard model of the universe, called Lambda CDM. Lambda for dark energy, CDM for cold dark matter.

problem-4-294bvx.text: It works beautifully. But it comes with two embarrassing problems.

problem-5-10osgcu.text: First, quantum physics predicts a vacuum energy too big by a factor of one followed by a hundred and twenty zeros.

problem-6-1f3hl51.text: Second, why is dark energy about equal to matter right now, of all the moments we could be living in?

problem-7-yvdjdx.text: Fitting the data is not the same as explaining it.

beyond-1-1osqtr7.text: Everything we can ever see fits in a sphere about forty-six billion light-years in radius.

beyond-2-bro0jl.text: Standard cosmology assumes that beyond our horizon, there's just more of the same: galaxies like ours, in every direction, forever.

beyond-3-kzjvwj.text: But what if it only goes so far? Out to the edge of what the Big Bang threw out, and beyond that, empty space.

beyond-4-1q7v3n8.text: Picture giant dark masses far beyond our horizon, each hundreds to thousands of times heavier than our entire observable universe.

beyond-6-ixr161.text: They don't form a neat grid. They form a lumpy, settled swarm, like galaxies in a relaxed cluster, only absurdly bigger.

beyond-7-7axggf.text: Physicists call that virialized. Not a frozen crystal where everything sits still, but a swarm where everything keeps moving, and the whole thing keeps its shape.

beyond-8-1irtfh2.text: And our universe sits in one of the gaps.

tides-0-dmf268.text: Here's a gravity fact that sounds wrong. Surround yourself with a perfectly smooth shell of mass, and it won't pull you at all.

tides-1-1rpl3os.text: Every direction cancels out. That's Newton's shell theorem.

tides-2-1xrcanj.text: But clumps don't cancel. The side of our universe facing a clump gets pulled harder than the far side, so it gets pulled apart.

tides-3-1phr4v7.text: And real clumps come in different sizes, at different distances. That makes the pull even more lopsided.

tides-4-y3p8pl.text: An outward pull that gets stronger the farther out you go. That is exactly what dark energy seems to do.

tides-5-16t9jrg.text: So to gravity, a pull from outside can look just like a push from inside. No exotic energy required.

whatif-center-0-b8hf13.text: What if we sat exactly in the middle, with the neighbours spread evenly all around us?

whatif-center-1-bonbm8.text: Then every pull would cancel out, and nothing would speed up.

whatif-center-2-f2me4y.text: But a real swarm is never perfectly even. One side always pulls a little harder.

whatif-center-3-1nyp6lb.text: So our universe should expand a little faster in one direction. Keep that in mind. It's a fingerprint we can actually look for.

progenitor-0-r0shgp.text: But wait. Why would we be anywhere near the middle of a gap?

progenitor-1-173gayu.text: What if the Big Bang was one of these attractors?

progenitor-2-swkkxx.text: Picture one of them, sitting at its balance point among its neighbours.

progenitor-4-s5hqz5.text: It blows apart, and its matter spreads out evenly into the surrounding gap.

progenitor-5-10rmmeh.text: That explains why we start near the middle, and why the expansion looks the same in every direction.

progenitor-6-13glblv.text: This is the Progenitor Hypothesis. And it means one mass plays two roles.

progenitor-7-m5on2r.text: Before the bang, it was one member of the swarm. After the bang, that same mass became our whole universe, plus whatever lies beyond what we can see.

progenitor-8-15nayut.text: The most natural guess is that our progenitor was just a typical member. Nothing special.

simulation-0-15vlykp.text: Nice story. But does it actually work? Time to simulate.

simulation-1-1t5cm56.text: We take thousands of particles in a cloud, and nothing but plain Newtonian gravity.

simulation-2-14aje9r.text: The cloud's own gravity slows it down. The distant attractors pull it apart.

simulation-3-f2tjaz.text: We start two point nine billion years after the Big Bang, and run all the way to today, thirteen point eight billion years.

simulation-4-3llpz2.text: First, a sanity check. We set the attractor mass to zero.

simulation-5-1vnhrh.text: The simulation gives back the textbook universe with no dark energy. Exactly.

simulation-6-16d6xle.text: Good. Now we turn the attractors on.

simulation-7-1dhsk4s.text: The cloud grows by just the right amount, like a universe with dark energy. Without any.

data-0-158r826.text: Now, the moment of truth: real data.

data-1-1e04bex.text: More than fifteen hundred type 1A supernovas, from the Pantheon plus catalogue.

data-2-1a4rh13.text: This is the same kind of data that gave Lambda CDM its numbers in the first place. Now we hold our simulation up to it, the exact same way.

data-3-gkcsa5.text: We turn the simulated expansion into a curve of distance versus redshift, straight from the particles.

data-4-fqemvz.text: Now zoom in on the differences. A universe without dark energy misses. Badly.

data-8-1dpa2d5.text: Here's the fit score, where lower is better. No dark energy: zero point eight four three. Lambda CDM: zero point four three six. Our model: zero point four four zero.

data-9-8pi5k3.text: Some runs even score zero point four three three, a hair better than Lambda CDM. But that gap is smaller than the simulation's own noise, so the honest word is: it matches.

data-10-1s46st1.text: And with enough tuning, some other setup would surely score even better. But that would prove nothing.

data-11-19igznc.text: As a software developer, this is something I watch for all the time. It's called overfitting. Give a model enough knobs, and it will fit almost anything. Simulations can fall into the same trap.

data-12-1lb1ezr.text: Fitting is not explaining. So a good fit is only the first test. Next, we check whether the simulated universe actually looks like ours.

whatif-observer-0-1ruqtam.text: What if we're not at the centre of the cloud? We almost certainly aren't.

whatif-observer-1-ldodyn.text: So every particle gets a turn being us. Does any vantage point see a universe like ours?

whatif-observer-2-1tjtwvk.text: Plenty do. And not in just one lucky setup. Across seventy-one configurations, the best vantage lands right around Lambda CDM.

whatif-close-0-sgoryr.text: What if the attractors are too close? Two things can go wrong.

whatif-close-1-jazkcu.text: The pull can win outright, in a runaway that rips the cloud apart way too fast.

whatif-close-2-mrwvha.text: Or something sneakier happens. The core of the cloud collapses into a dense knot.

whatif-close-3-klscwz.text: On the left, a run with a decent supernova fit, and a collapsing core. On the right, a healthy one.

whatif-close-4-990orb.text: So a good fit isn't enough. A universe-like run has to pass a checklist.

whatif-close-5-mhgk83.text: It must fit the supernovas, grow by the right amount, keep its core from collapsing, and keep every attractor outside our horizon.

whatif-close-6-2dcsgb.text: Picking runs by fit alone would have chosen the collapsing universes. The checklist catches them.

whatif-close-7-174pph5.text: We ran thousands of simulations to map where universes like ours can form. Inside the best region, we re-ran 72 configurations with more particles, and 68 of them pass the whole checklist.

whatif-mass-0-1kax4ys.text: What if the progenitor was tiny? Or enormous?

whatif-mass-1-a4a50r.text: We tried more than three orders of magnitude, from one observable universe up to three thousand.

whatif-mass-2-ueos8x.text: The fit barely cares. The structure does.

whatif-mass-3-12r6v5h.text: And the most robust choice is the typical member, exactly what the hypothesis preferred before we ran anything.

catch-0-3pcs3h.text: Now, the catch. Because there is one.

catch-1-6h7dtd.text: Heavy attractors far away, or lighter ones closer in. The supernovas can't tell them apart.

catch-2-tpsmsf.text: The average expansion only measures the mass divided by the spacing cubed.

catch-3-1bhawr2.text: So the supernovas alone will never prove this model. We need a different test.

predictions-0-1dazm0o.text: Remember that lopsided fingerprint? That's the test.

predictions-1-k0tmdp.text: Prediction one: a Hubble dipole. One half of the sky should expand a little faster than the other.

predictions-2-1yfnlxj.text: Measure the expansion rate from the whole sky at once, and you get 67. Measure it with nearby galaxies, and you get 73.

predictions-3-11jssxd.text: Those numbers should agree, and they don't. It's called the Hubble tension.

predictions-4-1ynn2nb.text: For standard cosmology, that is a headache. For this model, it is expected. A lopsided expansion, what physicists call anisotropy, gives different answers depending on how you look.

predictions-5-mf0var.text: Prediction two: the Axis of Evil. The biggest patterns in the cosmic microwave background all point along the same strange axis.

predictions-6-1v6wca4.text: Lopsided neighbours could imprint exactly that kind of alignment.

predictions-7-1xnihuo.text: Prediction three: dark flow. Huge regions of galaxies drifting together, as if pulled by something we can't see.

predictions-8-bvy9po.text: Prediction four: the acceleration keeps growing. As we drift toward the attractors, their pull gets stronger, so the speed-up itself speeds up.

predictions-9-z4aol6.text: Cosmologists call that phantom dark energy. A cosmological constant can't do it, because its push never changes.

predictions-10-1gs046y.text: And the kicker: all four should point the same way, toward our nearest, heaviest neighbours.

whatif-invisible-0-1mvdxct.text: If these things are so massive, why can't we see them?

whatif-invisible-1-17zsk68.text: Distance isn't the answer. They're older than the Big Bang, so their light would have had plenty of time to reach us.

whatif-invisible-2-1cj0mze.text: The answer is that they have no light left to give. They'd be ancient black holes that swallowed everything around them long ago, and a black hole with nothing left to eat doesn't glow.

whatif-invisible-3-1a594qu.text: Even their Hawking radiation is absurdly cold: about ten to the minus thirty-three kelvin. That's as close to absolute zero as it gets.

whatif-invisible-4-1jfg6mg.text: Dark giants. Seen only by their pull.

whatif-cycle-0-mbjl6z.text: One last, wild what-if. This one is pure speculation, with no simulation behind it.

whatif-cycle-1-1jbcxue.text: An attractor bangs, and its matter fills the gap.

whatif-cycle-2-1jwi0as.text: Over eons, the neighbours swallow that matter.

whatif-cycle-3-1wy1l20.text: One of them grows too big, becomes unstable, and bangs again.

whatif-cycle-4-w9si88.text: Our universe would be one breath in a great cosmic metabolism.

limits-0-1q7qbls.text: Let's be honest about what this is. It's a toy model.

limits-1-1vwzfo0.text: Newtonian gravity in flat space. No general relativity, no early universe, no microwave background spectrum, and no baryon acoustic oscillations.

limits-2-doyjua.text: It doesn't claim to be reality. It claims that ordinary gravity can fake dark energy. And that's worth checking.

outro-0-diqyzd.text: So, if the Hubble dipole, the Axis of Evil, and the dark flow all line up,

outro-1-1szkkhe.text: then dark energy might not be a property of space at all.

outro-2-p4tixh.text: It might just be the neighbours.
